tier_reason: JMLR 14 (2013) MLOSS paper, peer reviewed, Tables 1 and 3 time mlpack 1.0.3 k-NN and k-means against sklearn, Weka, Shogun, MATLAB and mlpy on an AMD Phenom II X6 1100T; every number in claimed_speedup matches the tables. No public harness, compiler or flags for these runs and the authors are mlpack's developers, so B and not A.

corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed (JMLR 14, 2013, pages 801-805, machine learning open source software track) but written by mlpack's own developers. Numbers are from 2012-era releases (mlpack 1.0.3, then LGPL-licensed; competitor versions are not stated in the paper) on a 2011 consumer CPU, so they say little about today's scikit-learn. Only k-NN (k=3) and k-means are tabulated; 'other methods, omitted due to space constraints' are asserted to show similar speedups without data. The paper states neither compiler nor flags, nor which search algorithm or settings each competitor used for k-NN (mlpack 1.0.3 itself offered kd-tree and cover-tree search), so the comparison is not settings-matched on the page. Weka and mlpy are excluded from the k-means table because they cannot take starting centroids; sklearn's k-means rows from miniboone upward are 'memory' (out of memory), not timings. The later public harness github.com/mlpack/benchmarks (107 stars) states no CPU, compiler or flags and does not reference the 2013 tables. The live results page mlpack.org/benchmark.html and the later benchmark system paper were not opened here. The 2018 and 2023 JOSS papers contain no performance numbers except that compilation is 'often an order of magnitude faster' after dropping Boost. No comparison against TensorFlow or PyTorch exists in these sources.

notes: All quoted numbers verified in the PDF (k-NN miniboone 20.2045 vs sklearn 714.2385, about 35x derived; k-means randu 727.1498 vs Shogun 7443.2675, MATLAB 3117.5177, sklearn out of memory). Shortcomings: 2013-era versions, self-authored benchmark, competitor versions/settings and compiler flags unstated, only two algorithms tabulated. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 5.7k stars, not archived, last commit 2026-10-06.

tier_reason: Vendor (Intel) numbers in the sklearnex README chart and oneDAL README chart, not peer reviewed; the chart states CPU and software versions but no compiler/flags or per-estimator workload sizes, and the linked IntelPython/scikit-learn_bench does not identify the configs behind the chart, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: sklearnex README text: 'average speed up of 8.5x on training and inference', 'up to 100X'. README chart image (scikit-learn-acceleration.PNG, combined FP32 and FP64 averages): fit LinearRegression 48.5x, SVR 28.8x, Ridge 15.2x, SVC 14.6x, KMeans 7.7x, DBSCAN 3.0x, ElasticNet 1.2x, Lasso 1.1x, KNeighborsClassifier(brute) fit 1.0x; predict NuSVR 395.8x, NuSVC 377.7x, SVR 330.5x, SVC 236.3x, KNeighborsRegressor(kd_tree) 153.3x, KMeans 24.6x, ElasticNet 1.1x, Lasso 1.1x. oneDAL README: '3-18x increase in performance compared to the default Apache Spark MLlib' (chart: Implicit ALS 3.6x, K-means 7.4x, Linear Regression 13.8x, Correlation 18.1x, PCA 18.2x).
corrections.caveats: First-party Intel numbers on Intel hardware (vendor selling the CPUs), not peer reviewed, so C. The speedup is measured through the Python sklearnex wrapper on stock scikit-learn, not through oneDAL's C++ API, and runs on 64 physical cores of one socket, so part of the gain is threading against stock estimators that are partly single-threaded (for example libsvm-based SVC/SVR). Benchmark code is linked (github.com/IntelPython/scikit-learn_bench, Apache-2.0, 124 stars) but the README does not say which configs or data sizes produced the chart, and no compiler or flags are given, so it is short of A. The 8.5x average and 'up to 100X' are README text; per-algorithm values were read from the chart, whose largest bars (NuSVR predict 395.8x, NuSVC predict 377.7x) exceed the 'up to 100X' text, while several estimators gain little (Lasso and ElasticNet 1.1-1.2x, KNeighborsClassifier(brute) fit 1.0x). The Spark MLlib chart is older (Intel DAAL 2020 Gold, Spark 2.4.4, emr-5.27.0, double precision, 7 x m5.2xlarge, no benchmark code, no CPU model). The old repo URL https://github.com/oneapi-src/oneDAL now lives at uxlfoundation/oneDAL. The arXiv 1909.11822 scaling paper cited by the README was not opened (arxiv.org blocked).

notes: Both README charts were opened and every quoted number matches; claimed_speedup extended with the chart's largest and smallest bars (NuSVR/NuSVC predict above 100x, KNeighbors brute fit 1.0x). Shortcomings: vendor benchmark through the Python wrapper, workload sizes and flags unstated, threading included, Spark chart from 2020-era DAAL. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 652 stars, not archived, last commit 2026-10-06.

tier_reason: ROSCon 2014 slide 16 and the CSV in scpeters/benchmark (Apache-2.0, 16 stars) show the time ratio numbers, and the harness is public, but no CPU model, compiler or flags are given, it is a conference talk not a peer-reviewed paper, and it was run by OSRF, which maintains the ODE fork it measured; C.

corrections.workload: Time ratio (wall-clock time divided by simulated time, lower is faster; the inverse of the usual real-time factor) of rigid-body simulation inside Gazebo-classic: a stack of boxes with large inertia ratio (Benchmark 3, object stacking, ROSCon 2014 slide 16), and free-floating 1x4x9 boxes (Benchmark 1), 1 to 101 boxes in steps of 20, 10 s simulated at 0.0005 s step (Simbody at 0.001 s).
corrections.caveats: The benchmark ran inside Gazebo-classic, which always builds and links its own bundled ODE copy (gazebo-classic deps/opende, headers gazebo/ode/ode.h, unconditional add_subdirectory(opende)); the slides themselves mention features only 'in our fork of ODE'. The measured ODE is therefore OSRF's Gazebo fork, not upstream odedevs/ode, and the measurer (Steven Peters, OSRF) maintains that fork, so this is not an independent measurement of this repo. Both engines run through Gazebo-classic wrappers, so Gazebo overhead is included. Repo scpeters/benchmark has 16 stars; no CPU model, compiler or flags are stated; results are dated about 2014-2015 (ROSCon 2014, Multibody 2015). The slide numbers are rounded to one decimal and sit next to a stack-position-error plot in which Bullet's error is lower than ODE's for top-link masses of 1 to 1000 kg, so the stacking speed result is not accuracy-matched. In the free-floating boxes CSV the accuracy columns of ODE and Bullet are close (same linear position error, angular momentum error 0.00643 vs 0.00626, energy error 0.00623 vs 0.00679). Result is mixed and small: ODE is faster than Bullet in 10 of 12 box-count configurations (by about 4 to 25%) but about 3.5 to 7% slower at 81 and 101 boxes with collision flag 0. The peer-reviewed Erez et al. ICRA 2015 comparison of Bullet, Havok, MuJoCo, ODE and PhysX and the Boeing and Braunl engine comparison exist but could not be opened (hosts blocked). ODE's own site (ode.org) was blocked and its README gives only the words 'fast, flexible, robust' with no numbers.

notes: Slide 16 (0.4 vs Bullet 0.5) and all CSV numbers verified (101 boxes flag 0: ODE 1.58186 vs Bullet 1.47622, ODE slower). New shortcoming: Gazebo-classic always builds its bundled deps/opende fork, so the numbers measure OSRF's ODE fork, not upstream odedevs/ode (Topaz fork precedent; already C). Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause OR LGPL-2.1-or-later, 30 stars, not archived, last commit 2026-08-07; the 2026 Bitbucket-to-GitHub move date was not independently checked.
